chapter: The Famous Door, Billy May and the Palomar fire
title: Carlos Gastell: friend and personal manager
summary: Barnet recalls working briefly as Gastell's partner after breaking up his 1949 band, and Gastell's sweating, Hawaiian shirts and loyalty.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: Oh, that was in '49, when I broke the '49 band up, which is another story, why I did that. But I wanted out of the music business for awhile, but I went with him and I stayed with him about six months, six, seven months, just for something to do, to see if I'd like it. I didn't like it. Because you not only have your own troubles, you have everybody else's troubles. And I have the greatest respect
for a successful personal manager, because he must go through hell.
But Carlos and I became long and fast friends there ever after, and I really felt -- I can't remember feeling any worse when anybody went than I did when Carlos went.
I know, he was a very well liked person.
You know those articles in the Reader's Digest, the most unforgettable character? He would be one of those.
Did you ever see him in anything besides those wild Hawaiian shirts?
I've seen Carlos under every possible situation.
Did he own an unprinted shirt or a coat? I never saw him wear anything but those loud Hawaiian shirts.

Oh, he owned them, but Carlos was a sweat machine. Sweat would pour off him all times of the day, all seasons. He just was in a continual perspiration. He -- of course as you know, Carlos was rather on the stout side, and you know he wouldn't eat until midnight or 11:00 o'clock, and then he'd eat a tremendous meal and then go to bed. But I've never seen --I used to say "Carlos, who has the handkerchief
concession with you?" Because he was always in a sweat. A very nervous man, a chain smoker. But if he was on your side, boy, you had somebody on your side.
He's the only man in my life that I ever gave power of attorney to.
